title: Extrapolation method to optimize linear-ramp QAOA parameters: Evaluation of QAOA runtime scaling
abstract_summary: The paper introduces an extrapolation scheme to determine the two linear-ramp QAOA parameters (∆γ, ∆β) and the QAOA depth p for larger problem sizes by optimizing on randomly sampled small subproblems (˜N = 4,6,8,10) and extrapolating to N up to 28. The method is applied to portfolio optimization, feature selection and clustering, and compared against classical solvers; the authors report that LR-QAOA with extrapolated parameters yields an improved runtime scaling for portfolio optimization, while no advantage is observed for the other two problems.
methodology_description: The authors propose and evaluate an extrapolation-based method to set the two free parameters (Δγ, Δβ) of a linear-ramp QAOA (LR-QAOA) ansatz and to choose a suitable QAOA depth p, avoiding expensive full variational optimization. They formulate three combinatorial problems (portfolio optimization, feature selection, clustering) as QUBOs. For each full problem instance (N between 12 and 28 qubits) they generate 10 random sub-instances of sizes Ñ = {4,6,8,10} by randomly selecting variables. For each small size they run an 11×11 grid search over log10(Δγ) and log10(Δβ) (initial grid for Ñ=4: log10(Δγ)∈[-1,1], log10(Δβ)∈[-1.5,0.5]) at an initial depth p0=6, compute average success probability Popt across the 10 sub-instances, and fit the 2D landscape to a multivariate skew Gaussian to obtain x_opt=(log10(Δγ_opt),log10(Δβ_opt)) and widths sγ,sβ. Using the fit center and widths they recenter a reduced grid for the next larger Ñ and repeat up to Ñ=10. They then extrapolate log10(Δγ_opt), log10(Δβ_opt), and log10(Popt_max) linearly vs log10(Ñ) to predict Δγ, Δβ and Popt for the target N. To choose p they estimate total quantum runtime D = d·Nshots where d (circuit depth) scales roughly ∝pN and Nshots is taken as the median number of shots required to see the optimum (Nshots = log(1/2)/log(1−Popt)). They search a logarithmic grid of p (p∈{1,2,3}∪{⌊2^{i/4}⌋, i=9,10,...}) starting from p0, and pick the popt minimizing the estimated D. Final validation uses a noiseless quantum simulator to compute Popt and D with the extrapolated parameters; for some instances they further refine parameters by direct minimization starting from extrapolated values. Classical baselines (CPLEX, Gurobi, MQLib/Burer2002 heuristic, Goemans-Williamson) are evaluated by sampling 10 instances per N and measuring runtimes (5 repeats per instance) and fitting T∝2^{αN} to obtain scaling exponents.
experimental_setup: Noiseless quantum simulator (unspecified) used for quantum circuit evaluation; classical solvers executed via Qiskit/MQLib and external solvers CPLEX and Gurobi. Experiments performed on randomly sampled instances; quantum simulations up to N=28 qubits. Grid searches and fits run on small subproblems (Ñ=4,6,8,10); final validation runs on full-size instances using simulator.
dataset_used: Portfolio optimization: annualized returns and covariance matrices for German DAX 30 (as of 2021-02-01) computed for period 2016-01-01 to 2020-12-31. Feature selection: German Credit Data (UCI) with numeric and categorical features, one-hot encoded (up to 48 binary features). Clustering: synthetic Moons and Blobs datasets from scikit-learn (2D).

portfolio.preprocessing: Annualized returns and covariance matrices computed; QUBO built per Eq. (3) with risk preference q (used q=1 in experiments), budget constraint B = floor(N/2) added via quadratic penalty with prefactor A computed per Ref. [22].

clustering.size: N data points (used N in evaluation up to 100 for classical scaling; in quantum tests N in 12..28); 10 random instances per N
clustering.preprocessing: Compute pairwise Euclidean distances w_ij = ||x_i - x_j||^2 and form Max-Cut QUBO per Eq. (8).

overall_pipeline: Formulate each problem as QUBO (Eq. (2)); add budget penalty for portfolio (Eq. (4)).
For each full instance size N (12..28) and for each of 10 random instances: sample 10 random sub-instances of sizes Ñ ∈ {4,6,8,10} by selecting subsets of variables.
For smallest Ñ=4: run 11×11 grid search over (log10(Δγ), log10(Δβ)) at depth p0=6; compute average Popt over the 10 sub-instances.
Fit the 2D grid landscape with a multivariate skew Gaussian (Eq. (14)) to obtain x_opt and widths sγ,sβ; center and shrink grid for next Ñ and repeat until Ñ=10.
For each Ñ collect (log10(Δγ_opt), log10(Δβ_opt), log10(Popt_max)); perform linear fits vs log10(Ñ) to extrapolate to the target N, obtaining Δγ_extr, Δβ_extr, Popt_extr.
Estimate Nshots = log(1/2)/log(1−Popt_extr) (median shots to find optimum) and total runtime D_est = d·Nshots with depth d∝pN.
Search a logarithmic grid of p (p∈{1,2,3} ∪ {⌊2^{i/4}⌋, i=9,10,...}) starting from p0 to find popt minimizing D_est.

Validate extrapolated parameters and chosen p on a noiseless quantum simulator to compute actual Popt and D; in selected cases perform direct minimization of D starting from extrapolated parameters to refine results.

For classical baselines: for each N sample 10 instances, run each classical solver 5 times, measure time to find a solution (or best found when terminated), and fit T∝2^{αN} to obtain scaling exponents.

Total depth runtime metric D = d · Nshots with Nshots median formula used to compare scaling.

key_findings: [supported] The authors developed an extrapolation method that estimates linear-ramp QAOA (LR-QAOA) parameters (∆γ, ∆β, p) for larger problem sizes by optimizing only on randomly sampled subproblems of sizes Ñ = 4, 6, 8, 10.

[supported] The extrapolation method was applied (via noiseless simulation) to three combinatorial optimization use cases — portfolio optimization, feature selection, and clustering — for problem sizes up to N = 28 qubits.

[supported] For the portfolio-optimization instances studied, LR-QAOA with extrapolated parameters yields an empirical quantum runtime scaling exponent α ≈ 0.22 (i.e., D ∝ 2^{0.22 N}), compared to the chosen classical baseline (MQLib/Burer2002) exponent α ≈ 0.328, indicating a slower growth of the quantum total-depth metric in these experiments.

[supported] For feature selection and clustering (Moons), LR-QAOA produced scaling exponents α ≈ 0.46 and α ≈ 0.25 respectively, which are worse than the corresponding classical exponents reported (feature selection classical α ≈ 0.2; clustering classical α ≈ 0.061), i.e., no quantum scaling advantage was observed for these two use cases in these experiments.

[supported] The extrapolated LR-QAOA parameters were often close to locally optimized parameters found by direct minimization (the paper shows cases where extrapolated parameters give depths near the minima), i.e., the extrapolation effectively produced useful starting/fixed schedules in many instances.
[supported] For the portfolio instances the empirical success probability Popt achieved with extrapolated parameters remained roughly constant with N (around Popt ≈ 0.1) across the sampled N ≤ 28.

[supported] Empirical fits of the optimized QAOA depth p versus N yielded different dependencies across problems: portfolio p ∝ N^{~3} (fit exponent ≈ 3.04), feature selection p ∝ N^{~1} (exponent ≈ 0.99), and clustering (Moons) p ∝ N^{~0.5} (exponent ≈ 0.5) for the instances studied.

[speculative] The authors note that if Popt truly remains constant with N and p scales as N^{3} (as they observed for portfolio in this N-range), then the total quantum circuit depth D (proportional to p·N) would scale polynomially (D ∝ N^{4}), implying polynomial-time solution behavior for that problem family — a conjectural extrapolation requiring much larger N or hardware to confirm.

[speculative] The paper proposes that extrapolation-based LR-QAOA parameter selection could be a practical approach to avoid expensive variational parameter optimization in many settings, but generality beyond the demonstrated instances and sizes is not established and remains to be validated.

[supported] The study was performed on a noiseless simulator and the reported runtimes / depth metrics and scaling analyses exclude some practical costs (e.g., real-hardware noise, gate time heterogeneity, and the computational cost of the small-subproblem parameter searches), and the authors explicitly discuss these limitations.

[speculative] The authors' findings do not fully align with the previously cited conjecture (Ref. [17]) that constant LR parameters exist making p ∝ N sufficient; instead they find non-constant ∆γ, ∆β (algebraic dependence on N) in their experiments, so the broader conjecture remains unresolved and dependent on problem class and instance structure.
results_summary: The paper introduces an extrapolation method to determine the two linear-ramp QAOA parameters (∆γ, ∆β) and the depth p for larger problem sizes by optimizing only on small randomly sampled subproblems (Ñ = 4, 6, 8, 10). Using noiseless simulations up to N = 28 qubits on three problem classes (portfolio optimization, feature selection, clustering), the method often provides parameters close to local optima. For portfolio optimization the authors report an empirical slower quantum total-depth scaling (α ≈ 0.22) than their chosen classical heuristic baseline (α ≈ 0.328), and an approximately constant success probability ≈0.1 with N in the studied range. For feature selection and clustering no quantum scaling advantage was observed. The authors caution that claims about polynomial vs exponential asymptotics are speculative and require larger problem sizes, inclusion of practical costs (noise, parameter-search overhead), or hardware demonstrations.
performance_claims: Portfolio optimization: LR-QAOA empirical runtime scaling exponent α ≈ 0.22 (D ∝ 2^{0.22 N}) [supported].
Classical baseline (MQLib/Burer2002) for portfolio: empirical runtime scaling exponent α ≈ 0.328 [supported].
Feature selection: LR-QAOA empirical scaling exponent α ≈ 0.46 vs classical MQLib/Burer2002 α ≈ 0.2 [supported].
Clustering (Moons): LR-QAOA empirical scaling exponent α ≈ 0.25 vs classical MQLib/Burer2002 α ≈ 0.061 [supported].
Observed success probability for portfolio with extrapolated parameters: Popt ≈ 0.1 roughly constant up to N = 28 [supported].
Fitted depth scaling for portfolio: p ∝ N^{3.04} (fit exponent 3.04) in studied range N ≤ 28 [supported].
Fitted depth scaling for feature selection: p ∝ N^{0.99} (≈ linear) in studied range [supported].
Fitted depth scaling for clustering (Moons): p ∝ N^{0.5} (≈ sqrt(N)) in studied range [supported].

Extrapolation procedure used 11×11 grids per subproblem size and multivariate skew-Gaussian fits to locate favorable parameter regions; extrapolation was linear in log-log of subproblem size to predict larger-N parameters [supported].
Claim (speculative) that if Popt constant and p ∝ N^{3} persists, total depth D ∝ N^{4} implying polynomial runtime for portfolio instances — requires validation at larger N/hardware [speculative].
quantum_advantage_detail: The authors report an empirical indication of improved quantum total-depth scaling versus a chosen classical heuristic for portfolio optimization up to N = 28 (α quantum ≈ 0.22 vs classical ≈ 0.328). However, this is based on noiseless simulation, extrapolated LR-QAOA parameters derived from small subproblems, and a limited N range; parameter-search costs, noise and larger-N behavior are not settled. Therefore any claim of quantum advantage is tentative and speculative pending broader validation.
limitations: Study limited to relatively small problem sizes (N up to 28), so conclusions about asymptotic scaling are tentative.
Results obtained with a noiseless quantum simulator — noise, decoherence, and hardware errors on real devices are not modeled.
Extrapolation procedure and scaling conclusions rely on parameters obtained from small subproblems (˜N ∈ {4,6,8,10}); the validity of extrapolation beyond tested ranges is uncertain.

The comparison of quantum vs classical runtime ignores the computational cost of finding or validating the extrapolated LR-QAOA parameters (the parameter-finding overhead was not fully included in the runtime comparisons).
For some problem classes and instances (notably feature selection) the extrapolation scheme produced outliers and was unstable — it can fail for particular instances.

Choice of classical baseline: comparisons use MQLib/Burer2002 as the classical reference (selected for stability and speed), which may bias the comparison and does not represent all classical solvers' performance uniformly.

QAOA depth optimization and total-depth model use simplifying assumptions (e.g., circuit depth ∝ pN and median-shot formula) without accounting for hardware-specific gate times, varying gate fidelities, or measurement overheads.

When reducing portfolio instances to subproblems, the penalty prefactor A was kept constant while the budget B was adjusted; this reduction strategy may alter problem structure and affect extrapolation validity.

Fitting/modeling choices in the extrapolation pipeline (11×11 grid, skew-Gaussian fit, log-log linear extrapolation) may impose modeling biases and might not be optimal for all instances or problem types.
Only three problem types were studied (portfolio optimization, feature selection, clustering), so generality across other combinatorial optimization problems is not established.
[inferred] The extrapolation approach assumes that sampled sub-instances are representative of the full instance; this sampling may not capture global structure and could mislead parameter estimates.

[inferred] The work does not evaluate sensitivity of the extrapolation method to the number of sampled sub-instances (10 samples) — scaling and robustness with different sample counts are not characterized.

[inferred] The extrapolation method was validated primarily on instances drawn from specific datasets (DAX30 returns, German Credit, Moons/Blobs), so transferability across different data distributions is uncertain.
[inferred] The study does not consider hybrid classical-quantum strategies (e.g., partial classical pre-processing, instance-specific heuristics) that may affect practical runtime comparisons.
open_questions: Can LR-QAOA (with suitably chosen ∆γ, ∆β and p) actually maintain a constant success probability Popt with increasing problem size N for large N, such that runtime scales polynomially rather than exponentially?
How can suitable LR-QAOA parameters (∆γ, ∆β, p) be found efficiently and reliably for large problem sizes without expensive optimization of large circuits?
To what extent do extrapolated parameters generalize across different instances of the same problem class (i.e., is parameter transferability possible/useful)?
What is the effect of realistic noise and hardware constraints (gate times, error rates, connectivity) on the observed quantum runtime scaling and on the viability of the extrapolation method?
Does the observed indication of quantum scaling advantage for portfolio optimization persist for larger N (e.g., N ≥ 50–100) and over a broader set of instances and datasets?
Which structural properties of combinatorial optimization problems determine whether LR-QAOA (or other fixed-parameter schedules) can yield better-than-classical scaling?
How should the overhead (classical and quantum) of finding/validating circuit parameters be accounted for in a fair comparison of quantum vs classical runtimes?
Can alternative fixed schedules or combined strategies (e.g., other heuristics, Fourier/TQA, different ansatzes) outperform linear-ramp schedules or improve stability of extrapolation?
How robust is the extrapolation pipeline to choices in grid resolution, fitting function (skew-Gaussian), and extrapolation model (log-log linear)?
What are the limits of extrapolation from sub-instances: how small can subproblems be while still yielding reliable parameter predictions for the full instance?
future_work: Investigate larger problem sizes (beyond N = 28) to resolve whether quantum runtime scaling is polynomial or exponential; this will require large-scale simulation or access to fault-tolerant quantum hardware with ≈50–100+ qubits.
Develop a deeper understanding of which structural features of combinatorial optimization problems determine their hardness for classical and quantum methods.
Explore using the same LR-QAOA parameters across different instances of the same problem class (parameter transferability) and quantify when this is effective.
Improve and generalize extrapolation and scaling methods (e.g., testing alternative fit models, grid strategies, sample sizes) to increase stability and reduce instance-level failures.
Incorporate realistic hardware models (noise, gate times, connectivity) into runtime estimates and adapt the depth / shot model accordingly.
Examine the computational cost and scaling of the parameter-finding stage itself, and include this overhead in end-to-end runtime comparisons.
Study combinations of fixed schedules and variational refinement or hybrid classical-quantum preprocessing to potentially improve performance and robustness.
Validate methods across a broader variety of datasets and problem classes to assess transferability and generality.
Develop benchmarks and standardized protocols for comparing quantum algorithms (LR-QAOA and variants) with classical heuristics across varied practical financial tasks.
key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — LR-QAOA with extrapolated parameters shows improved runtime-scaling for portfolio-optimization instances (N up to 28) compared to several classical solvers in the authors' experiments.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Parameters for LR-QAOA (Δγ, Δβ, and p) are obtained via classical optimization on small random subproblems and extrapolated to larger problem sizes, avoiding full variational optimization on the target instances.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — The extrapolation scheme is presented as a practicable strategy to set QAOA parameters in the NISQ era, reducing expensive parameter searches and enabling simulations up to 28 qubits.
#limitation:simulation-only — All quantum evaluations are performed on a noiseless quantum simulator (no real QPU experiments), so hardware noise and device constraints are not assessed.
#limitation:qubit-count — Experiments are limited to problem sizes up to N=28 qubits; conclusions about larger-scale behavior rely on extrapolation from small subproblems.
#limitation:noise — The use of a noiseless simulator omits the effects of realistic noise and error rates that would impact success probabilities and the required number of shots on real hardware.
#limitation:no-empirical-validation — No experimental verification on physical quantum hardware is provided; claims about runtime scaling are based on simulator data and extrapolation.
contradictions: contradiction:classical-vs-quantum — The paper reports a runtime-scaling advantage for LR-QAOA on portfolio-optimization but explicitly finds no advantage for feature-selection and clustering tasks, contradicting any claim of a general-purpose quantum superiority across combinatorial problems.

contradiction:scalability — The reported advantage relies on extrapolating parameter trends from very small subproblems (Ň = 4,6,8,10) and validating up to 28 qubits on a noiseless simulator; this raises a contradiction between the claimed improved runtime-scaling and the unverified behavior on noisy hardware or substantially larger instances.
